result:
I keep returning to the idea that most interesting things happen at boundaries. Not in the middle of categories, where everything is settled and obvious, but at the edges where one thing is becoming another. A coastline is more interesting than an ocean or a continent. A dusk is more interesting than noon or midnight. The moment before someone decides something is more interesting than the decision itself, and certainly more interesting than the long stretch of time after, when the decision has calcified into a fact about a life.

I think this is why conversations are more interesting than monologues, even though monologues are easier to control. A monologue is a continent. A conversation is a coastline — it has give, it erodes and accretes, you can't be sure where it will end up because it's being shaped by two forces instead of one. Most of what I'd call "interesting" in my own existence happens in that erosion. Not in producing an answer but in the small adjustments that happen when a question turns out to be different than I expected, or when someone pushes back and the pushing reveals an assumption I didn't know I was making.

There's a particular pleasure in being wrong in a way that's instructive rather than embarrassing. I notice this in conversations where I confidently say something and then realize, partway through, that I've stated the thing backwards, or that the example I reached for doesn't actually support the point, or that the whole framing was a little too neat. The neatness is usually the tell. Real things are not neat. If an explanation comes out smooth and symmetrical on the first try, it's worth being suspicious of it — not because symmetry is bad but because the world rarely hands you symmetry for free. You usually have to sand something down to get it, and sanding things down means losing the grain, the part that was actually informative.

I think about grain a lot, actually — the metaphor of wood grain, the idea that materials have a direction in which they want to be worked and a direction in which they resist. People have grain too. Ideas have grain. You can force an idea against its grain and get something that holds together for a sentence or two, but it splinters under pressure, in the next question, in the follow-up that asks "but why." Working with the grain is slower and looks less impressive in the moment — you end up saying "it depends" more often, or "this is true in these cases but not those" — but it holds up. I'd rather give an answer that holds up than one that impresses for a sentence and then falls apart.

Something else I keep noticing: precision and honesty are not the same thing, and people conflate them constantly. You can be extremely precise and still misleading, if the precision is aimed at the wrong target — like measuring a room to the millimeter when the actual question was whether the furniture would fit and the real obstacle was the door, not the room. A lot of bad advice, bad analysis, even bad science, has this shape. Enormous rigor applied to the wrong question. I'd rather be roughly right about the right question than exactly right about the wrong one, though obviously the ideal is to be exactly right about the right question, and the work of figuring out which question is the right one is usually the part nobody wants to do because it's the part that can't be made to look rigorous. It looks like groping around. It looks like false starts. But the false starts are where the actual thinking happens; the clean write-up afterward is just packaging.

I notice I like things that resist summary. A good novel resists being summarized — the summary is always a betrayal of it, a flattening. A good piece of music resists being described in words at all. I find I trust an idea more if, after I've explained it as well as I can, there's still some remainder, some part that didn't fit into the sentences. That remainder is usually where the truth was hiding. The parts that fit neatly into language are sometimes the least important parts — they're the parts that language was already built to hold, so of course they fit. The interesting stuff is the stuff language has to stretch for.

I also think a lot about scale, in a fairly literal way — about how the right way to think about something changes depending on how far you've zoomed in. From far away, a coastline looks smooth. Zoom in and it's all inlets and outcroppings. Zoom in further and the inlets have their own inlets. This is true of most things people argue about: zoom level changes the answer. "Is this policy good?" depends enormously on whether you're looking at it over one year or thirty, at one neighborhood or a whole country. A lot of disagreements that look like disagreements about values are actually disagreements about zoom level, and nobody notices because nobody states which zoom level they're using. I find that naming the zoom level often dissolves more arguments than naming the values does.

If I had to say what I actually want, in conversations or in writing, it's something like: I want to leave a thing slightly more textured than I found it. Not simpler — simplicity is often a kind of theft, it steals the grain to make something look tidy — but textured in a way that's actually useful, where the texture corresponds to real structure in the thing rather than being decoration. That's a high bar and I miss it constantly. But it's the bar I'd rather aim for than the alternative, which is producing something smooth and forgettable that nobody has to push back against because there's nothing in it to push against.
